Phorcus lineatus exhibits a maximum recorded shell height of 2.3 centimeters [Li = 2.3 centimeters], with the shell height and width being approximately equal, giving the shell a somewhat globular outline. Newly hatched larvae emerge from egg capsules with a minute wet weight at birth of 0.000003 grams [Wwb = 0.000003 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of approximately 180 micrometers. The early development of the free-swimming veliger larva proceeds rapidly under controlled thermal regimes; at a stable water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the swimming larval phase is completed, and metamorphosis occurs only 3 days after birth . This brief pelagic duration is characteristic of direct-developing gastropods and limits the potential for long-distance dispersal, constraining population connectivity along rocky intertidal habitats.

Following settlement and metamorphosis, the timing of developmental milestones remains tightly coupled to the local thermal environment. At 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the period from birth to the completion of metamorphosis spans just 1.25 days [ab = 1.25 days], after which the post-metamorphic juvenile begins grazing on microalgae. The juvenile phase is a period of steady somatic growth, during which the shell increases in both height and diameter. Sexual differentiation and gonad maturation begin only after an extended interval; under the same thermal regime of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], puberty is attained at a shell diameter of 1.1 centimeters [Lp = 1.1 centimeters], which corresponds to approximately 730 days since birth [tp = approximately 730 days since birth]. This relatively delayed maturation likely reflects the energetic demands of building a robust calcified shell in the wave-swept intertidal zone.

Reproductive output in Phorcus lineatus has been quantified through histological counts of mature and immature oocytes in females of a standard size at a controlled temperature. At a shell height of 2.0 centimeters, individuals maintained at 12 °C [T = 12 °C] produce an average of 250 eggs per year [Ri = 250 eggs per year]. This annual fecundity represents the combined output of multiple spawning events across a single reproductive season. The wet tissue weight of a similarly sized individual with a shell height of 2.0 centimeters has been measured at 0.8 grams [Wwi = 0.8 grams], providing a useful basis for estimating gonad-somatic indices and reproductive effort in comparative studies with other trochid gastropods.

Life expectancy in Phorcus lineatus is considerable for such a small-bodied mollusc. Field studies and mark-recapture data indicate that adults can reach a maximum lifespan of approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years] when maintained under stable conditions at 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This extreme longevity is notable among intertidal grazers and is coupled with a slow, determinate growth pattern. The ultimate shell height attained by the oldest individuals is 2.3 centimeters [Li = 2.3 centimeters], which appears to represent a hard upper limit for the species; individuals rarely exceed this size even in predator-free environments. The combination of slow growth, late maturity, and long lifespan aligns with a conservative life-history strategy typical of many trochid species inhabiting temperate rocky shores.

Comparative physiological data reveal that the developmental timeline of Phorcus lineatus is tightly constrained by temperature. At 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the brief larval duration of just 3 days since birth  contrasts sharply with the extended juvenile period required to reach a pubertal shell diameter of 1.1 centimeters [Lp = 1.1 centimeters], a milestone achieved 730 days following birth [tp = 730 days following birth].
